in the neighbouring country. He was one of the earliest and most active promoters of Christianity in Bavaria and Upper Austria, which, in 774, he filled with bishops. He took part in the Council of Constance and in the wars of Charlemagne to establish the unity of the Empire. On the death of the Emperor in 768 he became the first archbishop of Salzburg.

During the civil wars which followed Charlemagne’s death (768-773) he sided with the Franks and in 773 became a cardinal. In recognition of his services he was elevated to the see of Prague in 776 and died about 778. After his death the archdiocese of Salzburg, then called Salzburg in Austria, was separated from Bavaria, since then called Austria, and transferred to his successor, Peter of Zweibrücken, who died in 812.

new challenge for the medical community.

This is the case with the Apple Watch. While the watch is intended for fitness, doctors are worried that it could trigger a heart attack. The device monitors a user’s heart rate, sending data to the iPhone that the watch is paired with, which in turn sends it to the user’s health care provider. This data could cause a false positive for a heart attack.

Doctors are concerned that the devices will create an erroneous response when the body is trying to recover from a heart attack. It could make the heart appear to be beating too fast, or even cause a heart attack.

So, what should consumers do? Let’s presume that the watch is not the problem. The problem is with the person. They have to be aware of their heart, know what it is capable of, and take the necessary steps to live a long, healthy life.
